To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

We have assessed for the very first time the effects on DNA methylation and transcription in an untransformel, differentiated human cell line of chronic depletion of the maintenance DNA methyltransferase, DNMT1.

(1) we have identified four gene classes most sensitive to loss of maintenance DNA methylation; (2) we have found a novel interplay between DNA methylation and polycomb repression; (3) we have identified a role for maintenance methylation in the repression of cancer/testis antigen genes.
we have assessed for the very first time the effects on DNA methylation and gene expression of chronic depletion of the maintenance DNA methyltransferase DNAMT1 in normal human fibroblasts.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding the role of DNA methylation in the regulation of the genome and its impact on human disease.
the identification of the biological functions of DNMT1, and in the process we have generated a novel tool for epigenetic studies in human cells.

the identification of genes and pathways which are particularly sensitive to the loss of maintenance methyltransferase activity, and the interplay between DNMT1, polycomb repression and transcriptional activation.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
DNMT1 depletion is a powerful tool for identification of genes that are sensitive to loss of DNA methylation in human cells.

DNMT1 is essential for normal human cell function, and its depletion has widespread effects that include loss of methylation at a significant number of genes and regions, with consequent effects on transcription, and an interaction with polycomb repression that is likely to be of significance in the tumorigenesis of DNMT1 deficient cells.
loss of DNMT1 activity is lethal, but that the effects of hypomorphs in a differentiated cell type can be used to identify key classes of genes and pathways.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
DNMT1 is required to maintain a normal epigenome in differentiated cells, with a major role in maintaining polycomb repression and a minor role in gene repression.

the maintenance DNA methyltransferase is vital to the cell, but the consequences of its loss are not as catastrophic as might have been anticipated, and the cell can respond by derepressing a subset of polycomb marked genes.

the maintenance methyltransferases are essential for the maintenance of the epigenome in differentiated cells, and that this is a dynamic process, in which polycomb repression can play an important role.
The main takeaway from our work is that
DNMT1 depletion in differentiated cells has a profound effect on the epigenome and gene expression, but this effect is not permanent.
the effects of loss of maintenance methytransferase activity are complex in human cells.
DNMT1 is essential for maintenance of methylation in differentiated cells and that the effects of its depletion are not trivial.
